source.title: Efficient Continual Pre-training by Mitigating the Stability Gap
source.authors: Yiduo Guo; Jie Fu; Hui-Shuai Zhang; Dongyan Zhao; Yikang Shen

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream task performance and medical perplexity during continual pre-training, providing evidence about whether task performance tracks pretraining loss in this setting. It does not fit or test the scaling laws themselves.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling-law work in related work, but those cited findings are not results of this study. Its own experiments do not fit power laws, predict larger-run losses, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token split. The continual-pretraining performance and perplexity trajectories are relevant to V6; the general-task trajectory during Pythia continual pre-training is recorded as a related finding not covered by the versions.
record.test_reason: In medical continual pre-training, the study tracks held-out medical perplexity alongside downstream task accuracy. It reports task accuracy falling while perplexity falls, then recovering. This bears on V6's claim that downstream performance improves predictably with pretraining loss, in a new setting (continual pre-training rather than pretraining from scratch). It does not fit any power law or vary scale, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested. Tranche is T3 rather than T2: it is a new setting, not a different method aimed at the same question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that continual pre-training shows a stability gap: an early drop in task performance, then slow recovery, even as domain perplexity falls. They explain it via plasticity versus stability gradients. They propose three strategies: multi-epoch training on a moderately sized subset, a high-quality subset, and a pre-training-like data mixture. They report these mitigate the gap and improve domain performance at lower compute, e.g. 36.2→40.7 with 20B tokens. Their Llama-3-Physician-8B is reported to beat open-source baselines and rival GPT-4 on several medical benchmarks.
record.recipe_differences: The study tracks task performance and medical perplexity during domain continual pre-training; it does not perform a parameter/token/compute scaling sweep or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that learning rate and training-subset size affect task performance in its continual-pretraining strategies; these are not scaling-law fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: General-task performance of Pythia-410m first drops significantly, then rises during continual pre-training on unseen RefinedWeb data (no loss reported).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream task performance can follow a drop-then-recovery (stability gap) trajectory early in continual pre-training.

fits_no_version.finding: Instruction tuning of Llama-3-8B shows a slight first-epoch drop in medical QA performance, then a rise (Figure 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A stability-gap-like initial drop in task performance also occurs during multi-epoch instruction tuning.

record.problems: The trajectory results are described qualitatively, with no numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The authors note compute limits prevented verification on larger LLMs; the study is about continual pre-training rather than direct scaling-law tests.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows for the scaling-law versions: the paper does not report those tests. Strategy comparisons and downstream benchmark tables concern the proposed continual-pretraining methods, not scaling-law fits or predictions.

untested.parts: Predictability from model scale; any quantitative mapping from loss to task score; pretraining from scratch; settings other than domain continual pre-training.
All: no power-law fits or sweeps over parameters, data or compute.
All: no extrapolation from small runs.
All: no shape comparisons at fixed parameter count.
All: power-law form not examined in continual pre-training or instruction tuning.

missing.what: Llama-3-8B after medical continual pre-training: medical perplexity significantly lower than base, but average medical task performance drops slightly (loss–downstream decoupling).
OpenLLaMa-3B general commonsense task performance during medical continual pre-training follows a V-shape while medical perplexity falls.
missing.versions: V6 (only if general-task vs domain-loss pairing is accepted; otherwise fits_no_version)

missing.what: Perplexity under the authors' strategies falls below the 50B baseline by epoch 4. This can be paired with the higher task scores in Figure 4 and Table 1 (40.7 vs 37.4).

record.verdict_notes: The link to V6 is indirect. The paper never frames its results in scaling-law terms, and the loss in question is domain perplexity during continual pre-training, not pretraining loss across scales. Researchers may reasonably treat this as fits_no_version instead. All trajectory evidence is qualitative (figures only, no numbers or error bars). The scaling-law citations in related work are not results of this study.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit or sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No predictions from small runs are compared with larger runs.
No compute-optimal allocation between parameter count and training tokens is measured.
No controlled comparison of architecture depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study examines continual pre-training and instruction tuning, but does not test whether power-law forms hold in those regimes.
Tests task-performance trajectories alongside medical perplexity during medical continual pre-training only; it does not test downstream predictability from model scale or in other training settings.
No scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations are fitted or compared across setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: OpenLLaMa-3B
rows.operation_detail: Continually pre-trained on the medical corpus; average medical task performance evaluated every 5 billion training tokens.

conditions.value: average accuracy on MMLU-Medical-Genetics, MedQA, PubMedQA, and MedMCQA

rows.measure: Average medical task performance during training
rows.baseline: Original model performance; numeric value not stated for this trajectory.
rows.value: Performance initially drops during the first 5 billion tokens, then gradually recovers and improves.
rows.note: The reported early task-performance drop occurs while the study reports that medical perplexity steadily declines; performance later recovers.
rows.check: Link and state are fine: accuracy drops in the first 5B tokens while perplexity falls, then recovers and exceeds the start. No trajectory numbers are given. The endpoints are in Table 1 on a slightly different task set (base 36.2 avg, 50B full-token run 37.4 avg) and could be cited as baseline and final value.

rows.subject: TinyLlama
rows.operation_detail: Continually pre-trained on the medical corpus; medical task performance tracked during training.

conditions.value: medical task performance; tasks as in Section 3.1

rows.baseline: Original model performance; numeric value not stated.
rows.value: The same initial-drop-then-recovery trend is reported.
rows.note: The text states that TinyLlama shows the same trend despite its prior training on 3 trillion tokens; trajectory values are not stated.
rows.check: Same drop-then-recover trend, stated in text only. Figure 2(b) does not say whether perplexity for TinyLlama was plotted separately, so the loss–task pairing for this model is inferred.

rows.subject: Models in Figure 2(b), not individually specified
rows.operation_detail: Medical perplexity measured during continual pre-training.
rows.baseline: Initial perplexity; numeric value not stated.
rows.value: Perplexity steadily declines during continual pre-training.
rows.note: The text describes the trend but does not identify the plotted models separately or give trajectory values. This contrasts with the initial drop in medical task performance reported for OpenLLaMa-3B and TinyLlama.
rows.check: Perplexity alone cannot show whether downstream performance tracks loss. It serves as the loss axis against which R1/R2 are read. The subject is likely OpenLLaMa-3B and TinyLlama (the Figure 2(a) models), but the text does not name them. The decline itself is clearly stated.

rows.subject: Pythia-410m
rows.operation_detail: Continually pre-trained on RefinedWeb data; average general-task performance tracked during training.

conditions.value: 100 billion tokens sampled from the 2021–2022 subset of RefinedWeb

rows.measure: Average general-task performance during continual pre-training
rows.baseline: Original model performance; numeric value not stated.
rows.value: Performance first drops significantly and then gradually rises.
rows.note: This is a trajectory over continued training, not a test of predictability from model scale or pretraining loss.
rows.check: No loss or perplexity is reported for the Pythia run, so it cannot speak to loss→downstream predictability. Keeping it under fits_no_version is correct.

relationships.condition: Domain (medical) continual pre-training of OpenLLaMa-3B and TinyLlama-1.1B, early phase (first ~5B tokens)
relationships.reason: Medical perplexity steadily falls (R3) while medical task accuracy drops, then recovers (R1, R2). Task performance does not track domain loss early in continual pre-training.
relationships.display_finding: Medical accuracy initially fell and then recovered during the first roughly 5B tokens, while medical perplexity steadily decreased.

relationships.condition: Llama-3-8B continual pre-training with the authors' strategies (text, Sec. 5.3; no row)
relationships.reason: From the text, not rows: after continual pre-training, medical perplexity is significantly lower, yet average medical zero-shot performance drops slightly. Lower loss did not yield better downstream scores.
relationships.display_finding: Medical perplexity decreased significantly after continued pretraining, but average medical zero-shot performance declined slightly.
